entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11335"/><div sID="gen20505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11335"/><hi type="bold">11. which if a man do, he shall ... five in them--</hi>not "by them," as though they could justify a man, seeing that man cannot render the faultless obedience required (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.5">Le 18:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.12">Ga 3:12</reference>). "By them" is the expression indeed in <reference osisRef="Rom.10.5">Ro 10:5</reference>; but there the design is to show that, if man could obey all God's laws, he would be justified "by them" (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.21">Ga 3:21</reference>); but he cannot; he therefore needs to have justification by "the Lord our righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>); then, having thus received life, he "lives," that is, maintains, enjoys, and exercises this life only in so far as he walks "in" the laws of God. So <reference osisRef="Deut.30.15">De 30:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.16">16</reference>. The Israelites, as a nation, had life already freely given to them by God's covenant of promise; the laws of God were designed to be the means of the outward expression of their spiritual life. As the natural life has its healthy manifestation in the full exercise of its powers, so their spiritual being as a nation was to be developed in vigor, or else decay, according as they did, or did not, walk in God's laws. <div eID="gen20505" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11336"/><div sID="gen20506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11336"/><hi type="bold">12. sabbaths, ... a sign between me and them--</hi>a kind of sacramental pledge of the covenant of adoption between God and His people. The Sabbath is specified as a sample of the whole law, to show that the law is not merely precepts, but privileges, of which the Sabbath is one of the highest. Not that the Sabbath was first instituted at Sinai, as if it were an exclusively Jewish ordinance (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.2">Ge 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>), but it was then more formally enacted, when, owing to the apostasy of the world from the original revelation, one people was called out (<reference osisRef="Deut.5.15">De 5:15</reference>) to be the covenant-people of God.<div eID="gen20506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sanctify them--</hi>The observance of the Sabbath contemplated by God was not a mere outward rest, but a spiritual dedication of the day to the glory of God and the good of man. Otherwise it would not be, as it is made, the pledge of universal sanctification (<reference osisRef="Exod.31.13-Exod.31.17">Ex 31:13-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.13">Is 58:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">14</reference>). Virtually it is said, all sanctity will flourish or decay, according as this ordinance is observed in its full spirituality or not. <div eID="gen20507" type="x-p"/>
